idiom_name: ScheduledExecutorService.scheduleWithFixedDelay over an AtomicLong System.nanoTime() stamp (Java 21: one virtual thread per watched flow)
implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent supplies the timing and dispatch: a single ScheduledExecutorService evaluates each subject on a fixed delay, while arrivals stamp System.nanoTime() into an AtomicLong, so what replaces the classic structure is the executor plus a monotonic stamp - the per-subject expectation, the alert state machine and the escalation stay application code. Use scheduleWithFixedDelay rather than scheduleAtFixedRate so a slow check cannot overlap itself, catch Throwable inside the task because an escaping exception silently cancels all future runs, and in production publish the silence as a Micrometer counter/gauge consumed by an alerting rule engine instead of paging from the watcher thread. On Java 21+ one virtual thread per watched subject blocking on a timed poll gives the same semantics with linear, interruptible code.
pitfalls: An unchecked exception escaping a periodic task cancels that task permanently and silently: the flow then looks healthy forever - wrap the body in try/catch(Throwable) and make the catch itself alert.
scheduleAtFixedRate catches up after a stall and can run checks back to back; scheduleWithFixedDelay is the correct shape for a monitor.
Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor creates a non-daemon thread that keeps the JVM alive during shutdown unless a daemon thread factory or explicit shutdown is used.
System.currentTimeMillis() is wall-clock and can step backwards with NTP, producing last-seen timestamps in the future; use System.nanoTime(), whose origin is monotonic.
A thrown Error (OutOfMemoryError in a check) or a blocked alert sink stalls the single monitor thread for every subject - keep the alert dispatch off the evaluation thread.
Sharing one executor across many subjects couples their liveness: a blocked check delays every other subject's evaluation.

variants.name: Java 21 virtual thread per watched flow with a timed poll
variants.implementation_notes: On Java 21+ the monitor becomes linear and per-subject: a virtual thread loops on queue.poll(budget) and treats a null result as silence, so the pending poll is the last-seen state and no scheduled sweep is needed. Virtual threads make thousands of such watchers cheap, and interrupting them on shutdown is ordinary thread interruption rather than executor teardown.
pitfalls: poll(timeout) returning null is normal control flow, not an error - but a null element (if the queue allows them) would silently read as silence.
Virtual threads are still unmounted only at blocking points: a CPU-bound check inside the loop pins the carrier thread and hides the stall.
